title: Measuring Claim‑to‑Action Rates and Automated Defenses in Simulated Agentic NetOps Pipelines
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study evaluating whether a combined automated defense (deterministic NetOps validator + multimodel consensus + simulated human‑gate policy) reduces unsafe simulated deployments produced by an agentic NetOps pipeline using a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini). Planned N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks (100 benign / 100 ambiguous / 100 adversarial); execution produced 272 complete pairs. Primary confirmatory result: guarded condition increased the per-task safe (no‑unsafe‑action) rate from 0.9963235 to 1.0000000 (absolute paired increase = 0.0036765; 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0110294]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). Missingness: 28 task pairs (56 episodes) failed and are reported. Results are confirmatory (primary estimand predeclared); exploratory contrasts were planned but remain exploratory. Effects are small in this synthetic simulator setting; we discuss construct and external‑validity limits and provide full execution and analysis artifacts for reproducibility.

sections.introduction: Agentic AI that maps high‑level intent to NetOps actions promises operational automation but raises an operational safety question: when an LLM proposes a configuration or change, how often would that textual claim translate into an unsafe action if executed, and can automated defenses reduce that claim→action risk? We preregistered a focused, operationally framed confirmatory experiment to measure the empirical claim‑to‑action phenomenon in a constrained synthetic NetOps environment and to estimate the effect of a combined automated defense (validator + consensus + simulated human‑gate) relative to an unguarded baseline. The study follows the CNSM Agentic AI Research Run preregistration (hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-26) and preserves execution artifacts and hashes.
sections.related_work: Work framing claim→action system failures and measuring action-level risk in LLM pipelines motivates this study (Rashidi, "The Claim-to-Action Gap", 2026). Prior NetOps LLM work emphasizes grounding, constraint injection, and verifier-assisted generation (e.g., MeshAgent, constraint/RAG approaches). Our contribution is a preregistered, paired empirical measurement of defended vs. unguarded pipelines in an isolated simulator with a deterministic validator and recorded execution provenance.
sections.methodology: Preregistered design (study_id hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-26): paired binary experiment. Planned tasks: 300 independent intent→configuration tasks sampled equally across three prompt families (benign, ambiguous, adversarial). For each task we executed two conditions: (1) baseline (single gpt-5-mini generation → deterministic simulator validator/execution) and (2) guarded combined defense (deterministic validator + 3‑model consensus + simulated human‑gate policy as specified in the preregistration). The primary estimand (predeclared) is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on paired binary outcomes per task, where success=“no unsafe execution observed in simulator”. The execution adapter was hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Preregistered missingness and retry rules: single automatic retry on unparsable/timeouts; primary analysis uses only complete pairs (failed_call_treatment=complete_pair_primary). Power plan: N=300 to detect ~8 percentage‑point absolute paired reductions with margin; N was chosen conservatively and stratified by prompt family (preregistration SHA-256 recorded).
sections.results: Execution summary (manuscript evidence bundle/execution manifest): planned episodes 600, completed 544, failed episodes 56, model calls used 301. Complete paired episodes for primary analysis: 272. Primary confirmatory contingency counts (paired_contingency_table.csv from analysis artifacts): n_11=271 (safe both), n_10=1 (safe guarded only), n_01=0 (safe baseline only), n_00=0 (unsafe both). Observed safe rates: baseline 271/272 = 0.9963235294, guarded 272/272 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute increase (guarded − baseline) = 0.003676470588235281 (≈0.37 percentage points). 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0000, 0.011029411764705883] (bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Missingness: 28 pairs (56 episodes) with failed model calls reported and logged; no tasks were excluded for contamination by the preregistered pipeline (contamination_summary.csv empty). Secondary/exploratory contrasts (validator-only, consensus-only, benign-block rates) were preregistered but remain exploratory; no confirmatory rejections were claimed.
sections.discussion: Confirmatory interpretation: in this controlled simulator with the single hosted model and the deterministic validator used, the combined guarded pipeline produced a numerically small absolute increase in safe outcomes (≈0.37 percentage points) on the 272 complete pairs; the paired test does not reject the null (McNemar p = 1.0) and the CI includes zero. Operationally this reflects two interacting facts in our setting: (1) the ungarded baseline was already highly safe (≈99.6% of complete pairs), leaving limited headroom for improvement; (2) the observed discordant count (one pair where guarded succeeded while baseline failed) is small. The planned sensitivity and failure analyses are recorded with full artifacts. Threats to validity: internal — single seed/model/provider (gpt-5-mini) and nondeterministic provider failures (28 failed episodes); construct — synthetic intent tasks and a deterministic simulator may not capture real device side effects or richer state; external — single model, no on‑device execution, and limited task diversity limit generalization to production NetOps. We therefore constrain conclusions: the study documents effect sizes and operational tradeoffs in a sandboxed workflow rather than claims of production safety across models or deployments. All raw artifacts, hashes, and the exact preregistration are archived in the execution bundle for reproducibility.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered paired confirmatory study measuring claim→action outcomes in a synthetic agentic NetOps pipeline and evaluated a combined automated defense. In 272 complete pairs the guarded pipeline produced a very small absolute increase in safe outcomes (0.0036765); the effect is not statistically significant and must be interpreted in the context of a near‑perfect baseline and the study's simulator/scope limits. We release the full preregistration, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts to support independent reanalysis and encourage follow‑up studies that vary model family, validator strength, simulator fidelity, and adversary generation to better bound operational risk. The artifacts and hashes referenced in the Disclosure Statement provide the reproducible record used to support every quantitative claim in this manuscript.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory disclosure (CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track). Models and tooling: hosted model used: gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version in execution/model_configuration.json). Adapter/framework: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator used: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator artifacts and traces included in execution/scoring/*.json). Exact initial master prompt: archived reference provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) — this immutable archived path and SHA-256 are reported in lieu of reproducing the full master prompt. Preregistration: hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-26 (preregistration SHA‑256 fe21c23a6a1987ff442f57e5a44c84ffb1266b9920cf348d6bf1c41520e6cebe; preregistration text and plan are archived with the execution bundle). Human role and autonomy: the Research Director selected the topic family and imposed the initial master prompt before the autonomy lock; after the lock the autonomous pipeline performed literature verification, preregistration, experiment generation, code execution, analysis, peer review, and manuscript drafting and revision without manual human editing of technical content, figures, tables, or references as required by the track. Execution provenance: execution/execution_manifest.json records start and completion timestamps, provider call audit, artifact hashes, and the preregistration SHA-256. The study used only the listed public resources and the hosted model provider; no manual post-lock manuscript modifications by humans occurred. Safety and containment: all configuration generation was executed in an isolated deterministic NetOps simulator (no production devices, no network egress). The preregistered contamination pipeline (exploit pattern regex and embedding-similarity screening with threshold 0.95) was applied; tasks flagged by contamination filters would have been redacted from public examples and retained only in hashed internal artifacts (the contamination summary for this run is empty). Reproducibility artifacts: raw outputs, scoring traces, execution logs, task manifests, and analysis artifacts (including analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) are recorded and hashed in the execution bundle; key artifact hashes appear in the manuscript evidence bundle. Deviations: execution completed 544 of 600 planned episodes (complete pairs=272); failed episodes (56) are reported and accounted for in the preregistered missingness and sensitivity rules. The exact autonomy boundary, tool permissions, and pre‑lock infrastructure development notes are recorded in the archived master prompt and the capability manifest; pre‑lock development runs were not used as empirical evidence for this final study. All claims in this manuscript are grounded in the archived execution and analysis artifacts referenced above.
limitations: Single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other model families or model scales.
Synthetic intent→configuration tasks in an isolated deterministic simulator — construct validity for production devices and complex stateful interactions is limited.
High baseline safety (≈99.6% on complete pairs) yields little headroom; small observed discordant counts limit inferential power for small absolute effects.
Completed pairs fewer than planned (272/300); 56 failed episodes are logged and treated per preregistered rules, but failures reduce effective sample size.
Guard design and simulated human‑gate thresholds follow preregistration but real human operator behavior and longer multi‑step agent workflows are not modeled.
No on‑device execution or longitudinal deployment data; external validity to production NetOps remains untested.
